p.src: Grannie Liu held out both hands to show the size and said, “When the flower falls, it leaves behind a great big squash.” Everyone burst into uproarious laughter. After drinking the ceremonial cup, she joked again, “To tell you the truth, my hands are clumsy, and now that I have had wine, I may accidentally drop and break this porcelain cup. Bring me a wooden one; then it will do no harm if it slips from my hand and falls to the floor.” At this, everyone laughed again. Hearing this, Xifeng promptly said with a smile, “If you really want a wooden one, I shall fetch it. But I must warn you first: these wooden cups are unlike porcelain ones. They come as a set, and you must drink your way through the whole set.” Grannie Liu considered this to herself: “I was only joking to amuse them just now. Who would have thought she really had such things? I have often attended banquets at the great houses of country gentry and have seen both gold and silver cups, but never in my life have I heard of wooden ones. Ah, I see—it must be the little wooden bowls children use. She only means to trick me into drinking a couple more bowls. Never mind. This wine is as sweet as honey-water anyway, so a little more cannot hurt.” Having reached this conclusion, she said, “Bring them here, and then we shall see.” Xifeng then ordered Feng'er, “Go to the inner room at the front and fetch the set of ten bamboo-root cups from the bookshelf.” Feng'er acknowledged the order and was just about to go when Yuanyang said with a smile, “I know those ten cups of yours are still rather small. Besides, you said they would be wooden, but now you mean to bring bamboo-root ones. That would hardly look proper. Better fetch our ten large nested cups, each hollowed whole from boxwood root, and make her drain all ten.” “Better still!” laughed Xifeng. Yuanyang duly sent someone to fetch them. At the sight of them, Grannie Liu was both astonished and delighted. She was astonished that there were ten in a row, graduating in size: the largest was as big as a small basin, while even the tenth and smallest was twice the size of the cup she held. She was delighted by their extraordinary carving, all covered with landscapes, trees, and figures, together with cursive inscriptions and engraved seals. She hurriedly said, “Just give me the smallest one. Why are there so many?” Xifeng laughed. “With these cups, one never drinks from only one. No one in our household has such a capacity for wine, so none of us has ever dared use them. Since you asked for them, Grannie, and we have gone to such trouble to find them, you must drink from every one in order.” Thoroughly frightened, Grannie Liu cried, “I dare not! My dear lady, have mercy on me!” The Lady Dowager, Aunt Xue, and Lady Wang knew that a woman of her age could not stand so much and hastened to say with a laugh, “A joke is a joke, but you must not drink too much. Just have this first cup.” “Amitabha!” exclaimed Grannie Liu.

p.src: I would rather drink from the little cup. Put this big one away, and let me take it home to drink from at my leisure.” Her words set everyone laughing again. Yuanyang had no choice but to order the great cup filled to the brim, and Grannie Liu raised it in both hands to drink. The Lady Dowager and Aunt Xue both cautioned, “Slowly now—do not choke.” Aunt Xue then told Xifeng to serve her some food. Xifeng laughed. “Tell me what you would like to eat, Grannie, and I shall pick it up and feed you.” “How should I know what anything is called?” replied Grannie Liu. “Every dish is delicious.” The Lady Dowager laughed. “Give her some eggplant relish.” At this, Xifeng picked up some eggplant relish as instructed and put it into Grannie Liu's mouth. She laughed and said, “You eat eggplant every day, so taste ours and see whether we prepare it well.” Grannie Liu laughed. “Do not tease me! If eggplant could taste like this, we would have no need to grow grain—we would plant nothing but eggplants.” Everyone laughed. “It truly is eggplant. We are not teasing you.” Grannie Liu asked in amazement, “Is it really eggplant? I swallowed that bite without paying proper attention. Dear lady, feed me some more, so I can chew this mouthful carefully.” Xifeng obligingly picked up another helping and placed it in her mouth. Grannie Liu chewed it carefully for quite some time, then laughed. “There is a faint fragrance of eggplant, but it still does not seem like eggplant. Tell me how it is prepared, so that I may make some when I go home.” Xifeng laughed. “It is not difficult. Take freshly picked eggplants, peel them, retain only the flesh, and dice it finely. Fry it in chicken fat. Then finely dice chicken breast, fragrant mushrooms, fresh bamboo shoots, other mushrooms, five-spice dried bean curd, and assorted dried fruits. Simmer everything in chicken broth until dry, finish it with sesame oil, mix in some fermented-rice oil, place it in a porcelain jar, and seal it tightly. When you want to eat it, take some out and mix it with diced fried chicken, and it is ready.” Grannie Liu shook her head and stuck out her tongue. “Merciful Buddha! It takes a dozen chickens just to accompany it—no wonder it tastes like this!” Thus talking and laughing, she slowly finished her wine, all the while continuing to admire the cup closely. Xifeng laughed. “You cannot have enjoyed yourself fully yet. Have another cup.” “Heaven forbid!” Grannie Liu cried hastily. “That would make me drunk to death. I only love this beautiful pattern; however did they manage to make it?” Yuanyang laughed. “Now that you have finished the wine, tell us at last what kind of wood this cup is made from.” Grannie Liu laughed. “No wonder you do not recognize it, miss. Living as you do behind gilded gates and embroidered doors, how could you know anything about wood?

p.src: We country folk live as neighbors to the woods every day. When sleepy, we rest our heads against trees; when tired, we lean on them; in years of famine, we even eat from them. We see them every day, hear about them every day, and talk of them every day, so I can tell good from bad and genuine from false. Let me identify it.” As she spoke, she examined it closely for a long while, then said, “A household like yours would certainly possess none of those cheap, commonplace woods; you would never bother to keep anything so easily obtained. Judging from the weight of this cup in my hand, it is certainly not poplar. It must be yellow pine.” At this, everyone burst into uproarious laughter.

p.src: Just then an old maidservant came to ask Grandmother Jia, “The young ladies have all reached Lotus Fragrance Pavilion. Shall they begin the performance now, or wait a little longer?” Grandmother Jia hastily laughed. “Why, I had quite forgotten them! Tell them to begin.” The woman acknowledged the order and left. Before long, the mellow notes of flutes and pipes arose, joined by mouth organs and bamboo flutes. The breeze was fresh and the air invigorating; as the music floated through the woods and across the water, it naturally lifted every heart and refreshed every spirit. Baoyu was the first who could resist no longer. He picked up the winepot, poured himself a cup, and drained it in one gulp. He filled it again and was about to drink when he saw that Lady Wang also wished for wine and had ordered some to be warmed. Baoyu promptly offered his own cup, holding it to her lips, and Lady Wang took two sips from his hand. When the warmed wine arrived, Baoyu returned to his former seat. Lady Wang took up the warm winepot and stepped away from the table; everyone else rose too, including Aunt Xue. Grandmother Jia quickly ordered Li Wan and Xifeng to take the pot from her. “Let your aunt remain seated, so that everyone may be at ease.” Only after hearing this did Lady Wang hand the pot to Xifeng and return to her seat. Grandmother Jia said with a smile, “Let us all have a couple of cups. Today has been great fun indeed.” As she spoke, she raised her cup to Aunt Xue, then said to Xiangyun and Baochai, “You two cousins must have a cup as well. Though your younger cousin is not much of a drinker, do not let her off either.” With that, she drained her own cup. Xiangyun, Baochai, and Daiyu all drained theirs too. At that moment, Grannie Liu, stirred by the music and flushed with wine, grew so delighted that she began dancing about with both hands and feet. Baoyu left his seat, went over to Daiyu, and said with a laugh, “Just look at Grannie Liu!” Daiyu laughed. “In ancient times, when sacred music was played, all the beasts danced. Now we have at least one ox.” All the young ladies burst out laughing.

p.src: Presently the music ceased. Aunt Xue rose from the table and said with a smile, “I expect everyone has had enough wine. Let us go out for a stroll before sitting down again.” Grandmother Jia also wished to stretch her legs, so everyone left the table and followed her about the garden. Wishing to divert Grannie Liu, Grandmother Jia took her to linger for some time beneath the trees before the hill, explaining which tree was which, what each rock was, and the names of the flowers. Grannie Liu took it all in, then said to Grandmother Jia, “Who would have thought that in the city not only the people are noble, but even the birds are noble too! As soon as a bird comes to your place, it turns handsome and even learns to talk.” No one understood her, so they asked which bird had grown handsome and learned to speak. Grannie Liu replied, “I know that the green-feathered, red-beaked bird perched on the golden stand beneath the gallery is a parrot. But how has that black crow in the cage grown a crest like a phoenix, and how can it talk too?” At this, everyone burst out laughing.

p.src: After a while, some maids came to invite them to take refreshments. Grandmother Jia said, “After a couple of cups of wine, I do not feel hungry. Well then, bring the refreshments here, and everyone may eat whatever they please.” The maids went and brought two low tables and two small serving boxes. When the boxes were opened, each contained two kinds of delicacy. In one were cakes of lotus-root flour and osmanthus sugar, and rolls made with pine-nut kernels and goose fat. The other held tiny dumplings scarcely an inch long... When Grandmother Jia asked what their filling was, the old serving women hastily replied that it was crabmeat. Grandmother Jia frowned when she heard this. “So greasy! Who would eat such a thing?” The remaining dish consisted of assorted miniature pastries fried in cream, but she did not care for those either. She therefore offered them to Aunt Xue. Aunt Xue selected only one piece of cake, while Grandmother Jia chose a roll, merely tasted it, and handed the remaining half to a maid. Seeing how dainty and exquisite the little pastries were, Grannie Liu selected one shaped like a peony and said with a laugh, “Even the cleverest girls where we come from could not cut a paper flower as fine as this. I want to eat it, yet I cannot bear to. It would be better to wrap some up and take them home for the girls to use as patterns.” Everyone laughed. Grandmother Jia said, “When you go home, I shall give you a whole jarful. For now, eat this one while it is hot.” The others merely chose one or two morsels that suited their tastes. Grannie Liu had never eaten such things before, however, and since they were all made so tiny that even a pile of them scarcely showed on the plate, she and Ban’er sampled each kind and soon consumed half a plateful. Xifeng then ordered the remaining refreshments to be arranged on two plates and one assorted platter and sent to Wen’guan and the others. Just then, a wet nurse appeared carrying Qiaojie, and everyone amused the child for a while. Qiaojie had been playing with a large pomelo, but when she suddenly saw Ban’er holding a Buddha’s-hand citron, she wanted the citron too. A maid coaxed Ban’er to surrender it, but Qiaojie could not wait and began to cry. Everyone hastily gave the pomelo to Ban’er and coaxed him into handing over his Buddha’s-hand citron to her; only then was she pacified. Ban’er had already played with the citron for half the day, and now both his hands were occupied with fruit that he was eating. When he suddenly saw that the pomelo was fragrant and round, he found it even more amusing. He went off kicking it about like a ball and no longer wanted the citron.

p.src: After Grandmother Jia and the others had finished their tea, they took Granny Liu to Green Bower Hermitage. Miaoyu hurried out to welcome them in. Seeing the luxuriant flowers and trees in the courtyard, Grandmother Jia laughed. “Those who lead a religious life really are different. With nothing else to do, they tend the grounds constantly, so this place looks lovelier than anywhere else.” As she spoke, she made her way toward the eastern meditation hall. Miaoyu smilingly invited them inside, but Grandmother Jia said, “We have just eaten meat and drunk wine. Since there is a Bodhisattva in there, we might profane the holy place. We shall sit here awhile. Bring us some of your fine tea; we will drink one cup and then leave.” At this, Miaoyu hurried away to brew the tea. Baoyu watched closely to see how she went about it. Miaoyu herself brought Grandmother Jia a small begonia-shaped tray of carved lacquer inlaid with gold, decorated with a cloud-borne dragon offering longevity; upon it stood a small covered Cheng-ware cup painted in five colors. “I do not drink Liu’an tea,” said Grandmother Jia. Miaoyu smiled. “I know. This is Old Man’s Eyebrows.” Grandmother Jia took it and asked what water had been used. Miaoyu replied with a smile, “Rainwater collected last year.” Grandmother Jia drank half a cup, then smilingly passed it to Granny Liu. “Try this tea.” Granny Liu drained it in one gulp and laughed. “It is good, to be sure, but a little weak. It would be better brewed stronger.” Grandmother Jia and all the others burst out laughing. The others were then served in identical eggshell-thin, pure-white covered bowls of imperial ware.

p.src: Miaoyu tugged at Baochai’s and Daiyu’s lapels, and the two followed her out, with Baoyu stealing quietly after them. Miaoyu ushered the two into a side room, where Baochai sat on the couch and Daiyu on Miaoyu’s meditation cushion. Miaoyu herself fanned the water to a boil over the brazier and brewed a separate pot of tea. Baoyu walked in and laughed. “So you are having a private tea party!” Both girls laughed. “So you have come nosing after us to wheedle some tea again. There is none for you here.” Miaoyu was just about to fetch a cup when a Taoist serving-woman brought back the cups from the main room. Miaoyu hastily ordered, “Do not put away that Cheng-ware cup. Leave it outside.” Baoyu understood: since Granny Liu had drunk from it, Miaoyu considered it dirty and no longer wanted it. He then saw Miaoyu take out two other cups. One had a handle on its side and bore the three seal-script characters “𤫫瓟斝.” Behind them, in a line of small regular script, were the words “A treasured plaything of Wang Kai of Jin,” followed by another small inscription: “Seen in the imperial treasury by Su Shi of Meishan in the fourth month of the fifth year of Yuanfeng under the Song.” Miaoyu filled the jue and handed it to Baochai. The other was shaped like a small alms bowl and likewise bore three pendant-pearl seal characters, reading “點犀䀉.” Miaoyu filled this vessel and gave it to Daiyu. For Baoyu she filled the green-jade dipper from which she herself ordinarily drank tea. Baoyu laughed. “It is often said that all things are equal under the universal law, yet those two receive rare antiques while I get only a common vessel.” “You call this a common vessel?” said Miaoyu. I do not mean to boast, but I doubt that even your household could produce another common vessel like this.” Baoyu laughed. “As the saying goes, ‘When in a village, follow its customs.’ Here in your domain, gold, jade, pearls, and jewels must naturally all be dismissed as vulgar things.” Miaoyu was delighted by this answer. She found a great cup carved whole from a convoluted bamboo root, with nine curves, ten rings, and a hundred and twenty knots in the form of a coiling hornless dragon. “This is the only one left,” she said with a smile. “Can you drink this whole great bowlful?” Baoyu exclaimed eagerly, “I can!” Miaoyu laughed. “Even if you can, there is not enough tea to squander like that. Have you not heard that ‘one cup is for savoring; with two, one becomes a fool merely quenching his thirst; and with three, one drinks like an ox or mule’? What would you become if you drank this entire sea?” Baochai, Daiyu, and Baoyu all laughed at this. Miaoyu took up the pot and poured only about one cupful into the great vessel. Baoyu sipped it slowly and found it incomparably light and pure; he praised it without end. Miaoyu said solemnly, “You owe this tea to those two. If you had come alone, I would not have given you any.”

Both girls laughed. “So you have come nosing after us to wheedle some tea again.
There is none for you here.”
Miaoyu was just about to fetch a cup when a Taoist serving-woman brought back the cups from the main room.
Miaoyu hastily ordered, “Do not put away that Cheng-ware cup. Leave it outside.”
Baoyu understood: since Granny Liu had drunk from it, Miaoyu considered it dirty and no longer wanted it.
He then saw Miaoyu take out two other cups.

u.src: One had a handle on its side and bore the three seal-script characters “𤫫瓟斝.” Behind them, in a line of small regular script, were the words “A treasured plaything of Wang Kai of Jin,” followed by another small inscription: “Seen in the imperial treasury by Su Shi of Meishan in the fourth month of the fifth year of Yuanfeng under the Song.”
Miaoyu filled the jue and handed it to Baochai.
The other was shaped like a small alms bowl and likewise bore three pendant-pearl seal characters, reading “點犀䀉.”
Miaoyu filled this vessel and gave it to Daiyu.
For Baoyu she filled the green-jade dipper from which she herself ordinarily drank tea.
Baoyu laughed. “It is often said that all things are equal under the universal law, yet those two receive rare antiques while I get only a common vessel.”
“You call this a common vessel?” said Miaoyu.
I do not mean to boast, but I doubt that even your household could produce another common vessel like this.”
Baoyu laughed. “As the saying goes, ‘When in a village, follow its customs.’ Here in your domain, gold, jade, pearls, and jewels must naturally all be dismissed as vulgar things.”

u.src: Miaoyu was delighted by this answer. She found a great cup carved whole from a convoluted bamboo root, with nine curves, ten rings, and a hundred and twenty knots in the form of a coiling hornless dragon. “This is the only one left,” she said with a smile. “Can you drink this whole great bowlful?”
Baoyu exclaimed eagerly, “I can!”
Miaoyu laughed. “Even if you can, there is not enough tea to squander like that.
Have you not heard that ‘one cup is for savoring; with two, one becomes a fool merely quenching his thirst; and with three, one drinks like an ox or mule’?
What would you become if you drank this entire sea?”
Baochai, Daiyu, and Baoyu all laughed at this.
Miaoyu took up the pot and poured only about one cupful into the great vessel.
Baoyu sipped it slowly and found it incomparably light and pure; he praised it without end.
Miaoyu said solemnly, “You owe this tea to those two. If you had come alone, I would not have given you any.”

p.src: Baoyu laughed. “I know that perfectly well. I shall not thank you for it, but only the two of them.” Only then did Miaoyu say, “Now you are talking sense.” Daiyu asked, “Is this also rainwater from last year?” Miaoyu sneered. “For someone like you, you are astonishingly vulgar—you cannot even distinguish the water. Five years ago, when I was living at Incense-Coiling Temple on Mount Xuanmu, I collected snow from plum blossoms. It filled one demon-faced celadon jar. I could never bear to use it, so I buried it underground and opened it only this summer. I have drunk it only once before; this is the second time. How could you fail to taste the difference? How could rainwater stored from the previous year ever be so light and pure, or make tea fit to drink?” Daiyu knew Miaoyu’s temperament was eccentric, so she thought it best neither to argue nor to linger. When she had finished her tea, she invited Baochai to leave with her.

p.src: Baoyu said to Miaoyu with a conciliatory smile, “Though the cup has been soiled, would it not be a pity simply to throw it away? In my view, you might as well give it to that poor old woman. She could sell it and live on the proceeds. What do you say?” Miaoyu considered for a moment, then nodded. “Very well. Fortunately, I have never drunk from that cup. Had I used it myself, I would sooner smash it than give it to her. If you want to give it to her, that is your affair. I shall hand it over to you, so take it away quickly.” Baoyu laughed. “Naturally. If you were to speak with her and personally make the gift, even you would be contaminated. Just give it to me.” Miaoyu ordered someone to fetch the cup and hand it to Baoyu. Taking it, Baoyu added, “After we leave, shall I send a few young servants to draw several buckets of water from the river and wash the ground?” Miaoyu smiled. “That would be even better. But tell them to leave the water outside the gate, beneath the wall. They must not come in.” “Naturally,” said Baoyu. With that, he slipped the cup into his sleeve, then handed it to one of Grandmother Jia’s young maids, saying, “When Granny Liu goes home tomorrow, see that she takes this with her.” By the time he had made the instructions clear, Grandmother Jia had already come out and was ready to return. Miaoyu made little effort to detain them. She escorted them beyond the gate, then turned back and closed it. No more need be said of this.

p.src: Now, feeling weary, Grandmother Jia told Lady Wang and the sisters, including Yingchun, to accompany Aunt Xue to drink wine, while she herself went to rest at Paddy-Sweet Cottage. Xifeng promptly ordered the little bamboo sedan-chair to be brought. Grandmother Jia seated herself in it, and two old serving-women lifted it while Xifeng, Li Wan, and the assembled maids and matrons followed all around; but no more need be said of them here. Aunt Xue, for her part, now took her leave as well. Lady Wang dismissed Wen'guan and the others, distributed the compartmented food boxes among the maids, and took the opportunity to rest herself. She reclined casually on the couch where Grandmother Jia had just been sitting, told a young maid to lower the curtain and massage her legs, and instructed her, “If any word comes from Her Ladyship, wake me.” Even as she spoke, she lay back and fell asleep.

Even as she spoke, she lay back and fell asleep.

p.src: Baoyu, Xiangyun, and the others watched as the maids set the compartmented boxes on the rockery. Some sat on the rocks, some on the grass, some leaned against trees, and others settled beside the water; it made a very lively scene. Presently Yuanyang arrived to show Granny Liu around the garden, and everyone hurried after them to join in the teasing. When they reached the foot of the archway inscribed “Villa of Imperial Visitation,” Granny Liu exclaimed, “Goodness! There is a great temple here too!” With that, she dropped to the ground and began kowtowing. Everyone doubled over with laughter. Granny Liu said, “What are you laughing at? I recognize every word on this archway. Where we come from, there are ever so many temples like this, all with archways just the same, and the words on them are the temple's name.” Laughing, they asked, “Then what temple do you say this is?” Granny Liu looked up, pointed at the inscription, and said, “Doesn't it say ‘Precious Hall of the Jade Emperor’?” Everyone clapped their hands and stamped their feet with laughter, and still wanted to tease her further. Just then Granny Liu felt her bowels begin to rumble. She hurriedly seized a young maid, asked her for two sheets of paper, and began loosening her clothes. Everyone laughed again, but hastily cried, “You cannot do that here!” They quickly ordered an old serving-woman to take her away toward the northeast. The woman pointed out the place and gladly withdrew to take a rest.

p.src: Granny Liu had drunk some wine, though rice wine did not agree with her constitution. Moreover, after eating a great deal of rich, greasy food, she had grown thirsty and drunk several bowls of tea, so inevitably she was seized by diarrhea and had to squat there for a long while before she was done. When she came out of the privy, the wind suddenly intensified the effects of the wine. Old as she was, she had also been squatting for so long that, on rising abruptly, her vision blurred, her head swam, and she could no longer tell which way to go. Looking all around, she saw nothing but trees, rocks, towers, terraces, and buildings, and had no idea which way led where. She could only pick out a pebble path and follow it slowly. When she reached the buildings, she could find no door. After searching for a long while, she suddenly saw a stretch of bamboo fencing and thought to herself, “They have bean trellises here too.” Thinking this, she followed the flower screen until she found a moon gate and went through it. Directly ahead lay a narrow pool only seven or eight feet across, edged with stone. Clear blue-green water flowed away toward the far side, and a slab of white stone spanned it. Granny Liu crossed over the stone and followed the paved path. After turning two corners, she saw a doorway. She went in and saw a young girl directly ahead, coming forward to greet her with a beaming smile. Granny Liu hastened to say with a smile, “The young ladies left me behind, and I have been blundering about until I stumbled all the way here.” After speaking, she noticed that the girl gave no answer. Granny Liu hurried forward to take her hand, but with a thump she struck the wooden partition instead, hurting her head badly. Looking more closely, she discovered that it was a painting. Granny Liu thought, “So a painted figure can look so alive that it seems to stand right out!” As she thought, she looked and reached out to feel it, only to find the surface perfectly flat; she nodded and sighed twice in wonder. Turning around, she at last found a small door hung with a soft, flower-sprigged curtain of scallion green. Granny Liu lifted the curtain and went in. Looking up, she saw exquisite openwork walls on every side, with zithers, swords, vases, and censers set against them amid brocade cases and gauze covers, all aglow with gold and jewels. Even the floor tiles beneath her feet were green and carved with patterns. Her eyes grew more dazzled than ever, and when she tried to find a way out, there was no door to be seen. On her left stood a bookcase, and on her right a screen. She had just found a doorway behind the screen and turned through it when she saw her co-mother-in-law coming in from outside to meet her. Astonished, Granny Liu hurriedly asked, “You must have noticed that I have not been home these past few days. How good of you to come looking for me! Which young lady brought you in?” Her relative only smiled and said nothing in reply. Granny Liu laughed and said, “You really have never seen the world! Just because the flowers in this garden are pretty, you have covered your whole head with them without the least restraint.” Still, her relative did not answer.

p.src: Suddenly a thought came to her: “I have often heard that very rich families own a kind of full-length mirror. Could that be me inside a mirror?” Having said this, she reached out and touched it, then looked more closely. Sure enough, a mirror was set into the middle of an openwork red-sandalwood partition. She said, “But this blocks the way. How am I to get out?” As she spoke, she kept feeling around with her hands. The mirror was in fact fitted with a Western mechanism that allowed it to open and close. Quite by chance, as Granny Liu groped about, she happened to apply force in just the right place and tripped the catch. The mirror swung aside, revealing a doorway. Both startled and delighted, Granny Liu stepped through and suddenly saw an exquisitely appointed bed with hangings. By now she was seven or eight parts drunk and exhausted from walking, so she dropped heavily onto the bed, intending only to rest a moment. But unexpectedly she lost control of herself, swaying backward and forward with her eyes half closed; then, tipping sideways, she fell sound asleep on the bed.

p.src: Meanwhile, when Granny Liu failed to return, everyone waited for her, and Ban'er, seeing that his granny was missing, began to cry in alarm. They all laughed and said, “Surely she hasn't fallen into the privy? Quick, send someone to have a look.” So two old serving women were sent to look for her, but they returned saying she was not there. They searched everywhere, but could not find her. Xiren considered which way she might have gone. “She must have lost her way in her drunkenness and followed this path toward our rear courtyard. If she passed through the flower screen and entered by the rear door, one of the little maids would have seen her even if they crossed paths. But if she did not enter the flower screen and went farther southwest, all would be well if she found her way out; if not, she could wander in circles for a very long time. I had better go and see.” Thinking this over as she went, Xiren returned to Happy Red Court and called out upon entering, only to discover that the little maids from those rooms had slipped away to play while they had the chance.

p.src: Xiren went straight through the door and around the ornamental lattice screen, whereupon she heard snores rumbling like thunder. She hurried inside and was met by the reek of wine and flatulence. Looking around the room, she saw Granny Liu lying spread-eagled on her back across the bed. Xiren was badly startled and rushed forward to shake her awake without ceremony. Granny Liu woke with a start. Opening her eyes and seeing Xiren, she scrambled up and said, “Miss, I've done wrong! But I haven't soiled the bed or its curtains.” As she spoke, she brushed them off with her hand. Afraid that she might attract attention and that Baoyu would find out, Xiren merely shook her hand at her, signaling her not to speak. She hastily put three or four handfuls of lily incense into the censer and replaced its cover. After tidying up a little, she was relieved to find that Granny Liu had not vomited. She smiled and whispered, “Never mind; I'll take care of it. Come out with me.” Granny Liu followed Xiren to the little maids' room. Xiren had her sit down and instructed her, “Just say that you passed out drunk on a rockery stone and took a nap.” Granny Liu promised that she understood. Xiren then gave her two bowls of tea, and only after drinking them did Granny Liu begin to sober up. She asked, “Which young lady's chamber is this, to be so exquisite? I feel as though I've entered the Palace of Heaven.” Xiren smiled faintly. “Why, this is Second Master Bao's bedroom.” Granny Liu was so frightened that she dared not utter a sound. Xiren led her out by the front. When they rejoined the others, she said only that Granny Liu had fallen asleep on the grass and that she had brought her back. No one paid the matter any heed, and there it ended.

Instead, she seated herself in a light open sedan fitted with a bamboo chair and returned to her rooms to rest, telling Xifeng and the others to go and have their dinner. Only then did the young ladies return to the garden. To learn what happened next, listen to the explanation in the following chapter.
